Gangland fairytale

By: Anina Peens | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
From the heart of the Cape Flats Gangland, a story of inspiration about a little girl with big dreams

Unique Selling Point:
Eight year old Tamika van As does not have it easy in life. Growing up surrounded by gangs and violence on the Cape flats, Tamika escapes her reality by dreaming of becoming a figure skating champion, and she has reason to dream as she won gold at the South African championships in June.

Summary:
When bullets rain and little girls hide heavy weapons under their dresses, Tamika van As hides in her house, watching videos of ice skating. Growing up in the heart of the Cape Flats gangland means, Tamika can never play outside. In the backyard of her house, a colorful doll house overlooks the train tracks in Langa, the territory of gang leaders, vagrants and criminals. Tamika never plays in her dollhouse because bullets fly from the railway. But in front of the mirror in a small, enclosed area of the backyard, she practices her figure skating skills. Because Tamika is an ice-skating champion. The eight-year-old won gold at the South African national figure skating championship in June. Now, she is not only the number one child skater in the Western Cape province, but the reigning national child champion.

Further information:
Her family cannot afford professional ice time or skating time, so, her mother takes her to Grand West casino and entertainment world. Here she pays twenty Rand for Tamika to practice on the small children entertainment ice rink. During the 2020 lockdown, the rink closed, and Tamika had no access to the ice. Although coaching sessions were available via Zoom, the van As family do not have access to WIFI and was living off a SASSA grant because her father was unable to work. Tamika’s parents decided to end Tamika’s dream of becoming a champion skater, since there is no way to afford it.
But in March 2021, Tamika returned to Grand West to skate for fun. It was then that the coach from the local club approached her parents to enter Tamika into the national competition given her natural talent. Friends and family as well as Tamika’s school donated money for Tamika and her mother to travel to Johannesburg for the very first time. Her mother says she felt the funds raised could better be appropriated to put bread on the family’s table and not for some lavish rich man’s competition. She said, there was no way they expected Tamika to win as she had no serious training.
But to everyone’s surprise, Tamika competed against top skaters from five different provinces, and took home the gold.
The pandemic has once again, shut the doors to the Grand West ice rink, but Tamika says, this will not get her down. She dreams about representing South Africa on international level, but can only do that when she turns thirteen.

VIDEO: Dark: gunshots and people running use video material of gangs sent via wetrasfer. Lift the sound and add shots… merge with music as you move into the house and see Tamika sitting on the couch with her ice skating boots/standing in front of the mirror putting on her crown. Music must be classical sounding up from the gunshots and noise.

VO
Gang violence is a daily reality on the Cape Flats. When little children team up with their fathers and brothers in the gangs, eight year old Tamika van As, hides in her home in a backyard garage, dreaming about figure skating. Tamika never plays with the other children living in her neighborhood because many of them are part of the gangs.

SUPER@ RICARDO BENJAMIN: FORMER GANGSTER
“Die ma is miskien op dwelms, die pa is miskien op drank of hulle albei is op drank. Nou die kind sien daar by die merchant is ‘n uitweg. Die merchant kan vir hom ‘n paar skoene aantrek, die merchant kan vir hom ‘n tracksuit aantrek nou gaan join hy vir hulle en hy word n gunman”
SUBTITLE
“The mother is on drugs and the father may be drinking or they both drink. The child sees the merchant can give him a way out. The merchant can give him shoes or a tracksuit and that is why they join the gangs and become gunmen”

VO
Ricardo Benjamin is a former member of the Sexy boys, one of the most notorious gangs in the Cape. He is lives across the road from Tamika in Bonteheuwel and says violence on the streets can erupt at any time.

SUPER@ RICARDO BENJAMIN: FORMER GANGSTER
BYTE CHANGED SOURCE: 004890
TIMECODE06:50:10:09
“Al reen dit ook nou dit is die beste tyd vir hulle om uit te kom om te kom skiet”
SUBTITLE
“Even when it rains, it is the best time for them to come out and shoot”

LINK
Tamika is not only growing up in the heart of the Cape Flats gangland, she is also an only child and her mother does not let her play outside, simply because life in Bonteheuwel is too dangerous for a child. You are either part of the gangs or you are the enemy of the gangs. But when little Tamika is on the ice, the reality of the gangs and life on the Cape Flats disappear.

VO
Tamika’s mother Tarren keeps her distracted by taking her to an ice rink near Bonteheuwel.

SUPER@TARREN VAN AS: TAMIKA’S MOTHER
“We keep Tamika on the ice so that she doesn’t know what is happening in our community”

VO
She was introduced to ice skating when she was four years old. Her father who coaches table tennis was attending a marathon competition for three weeks at a nearby casino and entertainment center.

SUPER@ TAMIKA VAN AS
“I went to go visit my daddy when he was playing table tennis, he is table tennis coach. So, I passed the mini rink, so I wanted to play so I said mommy this look very interesting. So, she said yes but we are first going to visit your daddy. Then we went to visit my daddy then we went to the mini rink, and I played for a few hours, and I fell and fell but I got used to it.

SUPER@TARREN VAN AS: TAMIKA’S MOTHER
“We never knew what figure skating was about. It was the first time we actually saw figure skate because you know it was a sport that we never even looked up to or even saw. So, when she went onto the rink, and I had to sit there for three hours because she was playing on the little mini rink.”

VO
Tamika showed natural talent from the start and Tarren enrolled her in the local club.

SUPER@TARREN VAN AS: TAMIKA’S MOTHER
“About a month and a half later we saw a club at the ice rink. So, I took her to introduction day and the first day she got her two club badges.”

VO
Soon after, with her rapid progress, figure skating coach, Vage Evetts suggested to the Van As family that Tamika get professional training.

SUPER@VAGE EVETTS: FIGURE SKATING COACH
“She seemed to be able to grasp the concept and a lot of the elements quite quickly and moved through the first couple of grades quite quickly and that is when I realized that she has the potential to become a competitive figure skater.”

VO
But figure skating is an expensive sport and the Van As family was already battling to make ends meet. They had to pay coaching fees and additional charges for time spent on the professional ice rink. The only option was to pay R20 for three hours access to the mini-ice rink at the casino.

SUPER@VAGE EVETTS: FIGURE SKATING COACH
“She was such an eager beaver and wanting to learn and whenever I left the rink I would still see her on the little rink outside practicing and doing her stuff and I like to work with kids who want to skate.”

LINK
“Figure skating is one of the most expensive sports one can practice. And having parents who really battle to make ends meet meant Tamika’s dream to become a figure skater had to end when the lockdown came in 2020.”

VO
Tamika’s father Graham supports his family by selling school uniforms. During the lockdown, he had no income.

SUPER@GRAHAM VAN AS: TAMIKA’S FATHER
“Yo, it was quite tough because without money you cannot do anything, so it was quite tough to support my family but through the grace of God my mother and father and even my sister came to our rescue to help us with food and stuff like that”

VO
Tamika had to give up her classes and stayed home with her parents.

SUPER@GRAHAM VAN AS: TAMIKA’S FATHER
“We didn’t know how to tell Tamika she couldn’t go to the ice rink anymore. We had to cancel all her lesson with the coach, her ice time and even the Zoom lessons. There was nothing we could do, there were no other choice for us but to say no.”

SUPER@VAGE EVETTS: FIGURE SKATING COACH
“I didn’t see Tamika for about nine to ten months at all. We did some Zoom classes off ice whilst we were choreographing some new programs, but we could do nothing like that for Tamika because they didn’t have WIFI at home so that made it almost impossible, so I think for ten months I didn’t see Tamika.”

VO
At home in Bonteheuwel life returned to its daily reality.

SUPER@ RICARDO BENJAMIN: FORMER GANGSTER
“Every day it is the same story, elke dag is dieselfde storie, want jou kind mag nie buite wees nie. Tamika het nog nooit buite gespeel nie”
TRANSLATION

MASA QUESTION
“What is that like raising a child, let alone a very young small girl child in such conditions?
SUPER@TARREN VAN AS: TAMIKA’S MOTHER
“It is actually very scary me and Tamika was laying and it was seven and we were lying in bed and I said to her, Tamika you must listen, just listen to what is happening, listen to how they’re shooting. And she actually got up, and stood against the wall and held her hands up against the wall like you know someone that is scared for the shots that is going and I said, no, you have to lay down because when they shoot you must lay on the floor because if you stand they might shoot you but if you lay on the floor they won’t maybe reach you.
MASA
Is that the kind of conversations you have with your 8 year old child?....
VO
Tamika spent her time playing in the driveway of the garage and watching figure skating videos on her mother’s phone. But the moment the mini rink opened again, Tamika was back on the ice. Two months later she skated in the South African national championships and won gold.

VIDEO OF CHAMPIONSHIP UPSOUND WITH THE BEST MOVE?
VO
This surprised even her own family, because she was off the ice and attended no classes for a year.

UPSOUND OF VIDEO OF TAMIKA AT CHAMPIONSHIPS.

MASA
“So Tamika didn’t have these lessons during that period of time and then she goes to the championships and she wins gold.
SUPER@GRAHAM VAN AS: TAMIKA’S FATHER
“Yes, that was amazing, I think it was a month before they went, the coach phoned us and told us that she can maybe qualify.”

VO
Family, members of the community and Tamika’s school raised the necessary money for Tamika to travel to Gauteng for the very first time.

SUPER@VAGE EVETTS: FIGURE SKATING COACH
“Tamika competed at the juvenile competitive section and that is the section that she has won this year in 2021. There is a high-performance section for juvenile as well which I would like Tamika to move up to and then we are obviously going to look towards winning the gold there in 2022.”

SUPER@ TAMIKA VAN AS
“I felt proud of myself because all the hard work paid off, waking up a five in the morning.”

MASA
“And what are you dreams when it comes to skating?”
SUPER@ TAMIKA VAN AS
“I want to represent South Africa in the Athletics”

VO
She obviously means, the Olympics. But before she can represent South Africa internationally, Tamika would have to wait until she turns thirteen.

SUPER@VAGE EVETTS: FIGURE SKATING COACH
“Long term goals would be to move up the ranks in South Africa and get to further selections and go to junior grand Prix’s. But that is still a way off and we have a lot of work to do in-between. We got a couple of years though, provided Covid allows us to train.”

MASA: Tamika, what is it about the ice that you love so much?
SUPER@ TAMIKA VAN AS
“It is the costumes and the song, the movements, and when I go onto the ice and I put on make-up I feel like a princess.”



PROMOS

From the backroads of the Cape Flats, comes an inspirational story of a little girl who escapes her everyday reality in the ganglands of Bonteheuwel by living out her dream of becoming an Olympic athlete on the ice rink. Against all the odds, Tamika Van As became South Africa’s youngest figure skating champion. This is her story.

An eight-year-old girl from the Cape Flats defied the odds when she won gold at the national figure skating championships in June. We visit her at her home, a backyard dwelling in Bonteheuwel.

There’s no such thing as a normal childhood when growing up on the Cape Flats. But little Tamika van As is not concerned. She rather spends her time ice skating with one vision, to become an Olympic gold medalist. And she has reason to dream as she just won gold at the South African national championships at only eight years old.

SUPER@ TAMIKA VAN AS “It is the costumes and the song, the movements, and when I go onto the ice and I put on make-up I feel like a princess.” PROMOS From the backroads of the Cape Flats, comes an inspirational story of a little girl who escapes her everyday reality in the ganglands of Bonteheuwel by living out her dream of becoming an Olympic athlete on the ice rink. Against all the odds, Tamika Van As became South Africa’s youngest figure skating champion. This is her story. An eight-year-old girl from the Cape Flats defied the odds when she won gold at the national figure skating championships in June. We visit her at her home, a backyard dwelling in Bonteheuwel. There’s no such thing as a normal childhood when growing up on the Cape Flats. But little Tamika van As is not concerned. She rather spends her time ice skating with one vision, to become an Olympic gold medalist. And she has reason to dream as she just won gold at the South African national championships at only eight years old.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): From the heart of the Cape Flats Gangland, a story of inspiration about a little girl with big dreams
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Eight year old Tamika van As does not have it easy in life. Growing up surrounded by gangs and violence on the Cape flats, Tamika escapes her reality by dreaming of becoming a figure skating champion, and she has reason to dream as she won gold at the South African championships in June.
metadata.Summary: When bullets rain and little girls hide heavy weapons under their dresses, Tamika van As hides in her house, watching videos of ice skating. Growing up in the heart of the Cape Flats gangland means, Tamika can never play outside. In the backyard of her house, a colorful doll house overlooks the train tracks in Langa, the territory of gang leaders, vagrants and criminals. Tamika never plays in her dollhouse because bullets fly from the railway. But in front of the mirror in a small, enclosed area of the backyard, she practices her figure skating skills. Because Tamika is an ice-skating champion. The eight-year-old won gold at the South African national figure skating championship in June. Now, she is not only the number one child skater in the Western Cape province, but the reigning national child champion.
metadata.Further information: Her family cannot afford professional ice time or skating time, so, her mother takes her to Grand West casino and entertainment world. Here she pays twenty Rand for Tamika to practice on the small children entertainment ice rink. During the 2020 lockdown, the rink closed, and Tamika had no access to the ice. Although coaching sessions were available via Zoom, the van As family do not have access to WIFI and was living off a SASSA grant because her father was unable to work. Tamika’s parents decided to end Tamika’s dream of becoming a champion skater, since there is no way to afford it. But in March 2021, Tamika returned to Grand West to skate for fun. It was then that the coach from the local club approached her parents to enter Tamika into the national competition given her natural talent. Friends and family as well as Tamika’s school donated money for Tamika and her mother to travel to Johannesburg for the very first time. Her mother says she felt the funds raised could better be appropriated to put bread on the family’s table and not for some lavish rich man’s competition. She said, there was no way they expected Tamika to win as she had no serious training. But to everyone’s surprise, Tamika competed against top skaters from five different provinces, and took home the gold. The pandemic has once again, shut the doors to the Grand West ice rink, but Tamika says, this will not get her down. She dreams about representing South Africa on international level, but can only do that when she turns thirteen.
